notes.meaning: The writer asks God to give His laws and righteous character to the reigning king and his royal son. In Israel, kings ruled under God's authority, so they needed divine wisdom to judge fairly. While this prayer was spoken for Solomon, it points ahead to Jesus Christ, the Son who receives all judgment from the Father.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explains that the King is God the Father and the King's Son is Christ, to whom the Father has committed all judgment.

notes.meaning: A godly king must govern the nation with fairness and integrity. He is called to show special care for the poor and afflicted, defending them from mistreatment. In Christ's kingdom, the humble find true justice and gentle protection.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine views God's people and the afflicted as the same group, teaching that all of God's people are called to be humble and poor in spirit.

notes.meaning: The mountains and hills across the land are pictured as bearing a rich harvest of peace. When righteous government rules the land, even high and dangerous places become safe and quiet. Christ brings this lasting peace to human hearts through His own righteousness.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interprets the mountains as prominent leaders in the Church and the hills as their followers, who are called to promote peace rather than division.

notes.meaning: The king uses his power to defend the innocent and save the children of the poor. At the same time, he strikes down corrupt and violent bullies who crush the weak. Christ fulfills this work by rescuing His needy people and crushing the power of Satan.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine identifies the oppressor as the devil, whom Christ crushes to rescue His people.

notes.meaning: Godly rule leads the people to revere the Lord through every age, as long as the sun and moon remain. True religion flourishes when a king rules according to God's word. Because earthly kings pass away, this unending worship belongs to the everlasting kingdom of Christ.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explains that the sun represents Christ's body on earth, the Church, which will continue through all generations.

notes.meaning: The king's leadership is compared to gentle rain falling on pasture grass that has just been grazed or cut. Instead of trampling the people, his presence brings soothing relief and helps them flourish again. In this way, Christ pours out His Holy Spirit and truth to refresh drooping souls.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine reads the Hebrew word as fleece rather than grass, seeing Gideon's dew-covered fleece as a symbol of grace given through Christ.

notes.meaning: Under a righteous ruler, good people thrive and peace fills the entire land. This abundant peace is meant to last until the moon is no more. Christ is the true king of peace, giving His people security that outlasts every earthly trouble.

The prayer asks that the king's rule stretch from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates River to the ends of the earth. Solomon governed a wide realm, but these words describe a truly universal empire. Only Christ's kingdom reaches across the entire globe as the gospel spreads to every land.

Wild desert tribes will bow low in deep submission before the king. His enemies will be completely conquered, brought face-down into the dust. Every opposing power will either gladly yield to Christ or face total defeat under His authority.

Kings from distant coastlands and wealthy southern nations bring tribute and voluntary gifts to honor the monarch. Wealthy traders and foreign rulers gladly present their treasures to him. This pointed to foreign rulers visiting Solomon, and it foreshadows kings offering their wealth and devotion to Christ.

Every royal ruler on earth will bow down before this king, and all nations will serve him. No ordinary human ruler has ever exercised complete power over every nation. These words find their true fulfillment when all people acknowledge Jesus Christ as Lord.

Nations gladly submit to this king because he cares for those who are down and out. He hears the cries of the poor and rescues people who have no one else to stand up for them. Christ delights to help those who realize they have no earthly helper.

The king shows tender pity to the weak and shields the needy from destruction. He does not act like selfish rulers who exploit the poor, but instead preserves their lives. Christ is the Savior of souls, giving life and protection to all who seek His mercy.

He ransoms his people from deceitful traps and brutal cruelty. He treats the lives and blood of the poor as deeply precious, refusing to waste them in selfish pursuits. Christ guards His followers from the lies of enemies and counts every life of immense value.

Acclamations ring out for the king to enjoy a long, prosperous life, and fine gold is offered to him. His loyal subjects pray constantly for the success of his rule and praise him every day. Christians offer their devotion to the living Christ and continually pray for His kingdom to grow.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators suggest that the person who lives and gives gold is the rescued poor man from the previous verse, who now prays for and blesses his royal protector.

notes.meaning: A small handful of grain sown on a dry mountaintop will grow into a massive crop waving like the great forests of Lebanon. City populations will also multiply and thrive like lush grass in the fields. This portrays the marvelous spread of the gospel, where small beginnings produce a rich spiritual harvest worldwide.

The king's name and fame will endure forever, shining as long as the sun gives light. All nations will be blessed through him and gladly speak well of him. This fulfills God's promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would find blessing in his seed.

The psalm closes with joyful praise to the Lord God of Israel, the only one who works great miracles. His glorious name deserves unending blessing, and the prayer asks for His glory to fill the entire earth. A double 'Amen' seals the prayer, expressing complete certainty that God's promises will stand.

This statement concludes the collection of David's prayers at the end of the second book of the Psalms. Having seen the future reign of his royal line and the glory of the coming Messiah, David desired nothing more. His life and prayers reached their ultimate goal in the promise of Christ's kingdom.
